title: Pool cleaning frequency dispute
scenario: Riverbend Apartments CTS 40112. On Monday 5 October the committee secretary emails you: "The pool has been dirty all weekend. The caretaker must clean it daily – please instruct him to start tomorrow." Schedule 2 (Duties) of the caretaking agreement, item 14, reads: "Pool and spa: clean, skim and vacuum weekly; test and balance chemicals twice weekly." There is no committee resolution varying the duties. The caretaker's log shows the pool was cleaned on Thursday 1 October.
instructions:
1.	Identify what the agreement requires and whether the caretaker is in breach.
2.	State whether you can issue the instruction the committee asked for.
3.	Draft your reply to the secretary.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Read the full duty schedule (item 14 and any general clause on standard of work), not just the clause quoted by the committee.
2.	Check for any registered variation, deed or committee resolution changing the pool frequency.
3.	Check the caretaker's log and any photographs for the last two weeks against the weekly and twice-weekly obligations.
4.	Separate the two questions: (a) has the caretaker met the weekly duty, and (b) does the committee want a higher standard than the agreement provides.
Correct outcome: On the facts given, the caretaker is not in breach – the agreement requires weekly cleaning and the last clean was within the week. You cannot instruct daily cleaning because duties cannot be added informally. If the committee wants daily cleaning, the options are to negotiate a formal variation with the caretaker (with legal review) or engage a separate contractor for the extra work.
Example response
Hi [Secretary],
I've checked the caretaking agreement. Schedule 2, item 14 requires the pool to be cleaned weekly and chemicals tested twice weekly. The caretaker's log shows the pool was cleaned on Thursday 1 October, which is within that requirement, so there is no breach at this stage.
I'm not able to instruct daily cleaning, as that would add a duty the agreement doesn't contain. If the committee would like daily cleaning, we can (1) ask the caretaker whether he'll agree to a formal variation, which would need legal review and the appropriate resolution, or (2) obtain a quote from a pool contractor for the extra visits.
If the pool was dirty because of a one-off event (storm, heavy use), I'm happy to ask the caretaker to attend early this week as a courtesy request, not a direction.
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Quotes or accurately identifies the weekly frequency and concludes no breach on these facts.
- States clearly that extra duties need a formal variation, not an instruction.
- Offers at least one lawful option to get the outcome the committee wants.
Not yet competent:
- Passes the committee's instruction to the caretaker.
- Says "check the agreement" without stating what it says or the conclusion.

title: Garden maintenance allegation
scenario: Parkside Terraces CTS 38870. The committee chair writes: "The gardens are a disgrace. The caretaker is clearly in breach. Issue him a notice." Schedule 2 requires: "Mow lawns fortnightly (Oct–Mar) and monthly (Apr–Sep); weed and edge garden beds monthly; prune hedges quarterly." The chair attaches four photos taken on 2 October showing long grass along the eastern boundary and weeds in the front bed. The caretaker's last logged mow was 14 September.
instructions:
1.	List, in order, the documents and evidence you would gather before forming a view.
2.	State your preliminary assessment on the facts given.
3.	Draft a short email to the caretaker requesting his records.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Duty schedule: the exact frequency for each task and the season it applies to (October = fortnightly mowing).
2.	Any variation, deed or side letter changing garden duties.
3.	The caretaker's maintenance log / timesheets for the last two months.
4.	Photographs: date, location and whether they show areas within the caretaker's duty area (confirm the eastern boundary is common property, not a lot or a council verge).
5.	Prior correspondence: earlier complaints, warnings or caretaker explanations (e.g. mower breakdown, rain).
6.	Then compare: 14 September to 2 October is 18 days – in October the fortnightly requirement applies, so a mow was due by about 28 September.
Correct outcome: There is a possible breach of the fortnightly mowing duty, but it is not established until the caretaker's records are checked and the area is confirmed as within his duties. No notice should issue yet. Weeding cannot be assessed until you confirm when it was last done.
Example response
Hi [Caretaker],
The committee has raised concerns about the lawns and garden beds, with photos taken on 2 October. To review this fairly, could you please send me by Friday 9 October:
- your maintenance log for mowing, weeding and edging from 1 August to date; and
- any reason work may have been delayed (weather, equipment, access).
Under Schedule 2, mowing is fortnightly from October and weeding is monthly. I'd like to understand the position before reporting back to the committee.
Thanks,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Identifies the seasonal frequency and applies it to the dates.
- Checks that the area in the photos is within the duty area.
- Concludes "possible breach, not yet established" and does not issue a notice.
Not yet competent:
- Lists generic "evidence" without linking it to the duty schedule.
- Treats the photos alone as proof of breach.

title: Rewriting a vague duty
scenario: A draft variation for Coral Point CTS 29455 contains this duty: "Clean common property as reasonably required." The committee is concerned it cannot be enforced. The common property includes: main lobby, two lifts, five-level stairwells (east and west), basement car park, bin room and pool deck.
instructions:
1.	Explain why the current wording is hard to enforce.
2.	Rewrite it as enforceable duties covering area, task, standard and frequency.
3.	Note what must happen before the new wording takes effect.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Identify each area to be covered (use the common property list).
2.	For each area, state the task, the standard (what "clean" looks like) and the frequency.
3.	Make sure frequencies are measurable (daily, three times weekly, monthly) and can be checked against a log.
4.	Confirm the change is processed as a formal variation, not just an updated duty list.
Correct outcome: "As reasonably required" sets no measurable standard or frequency, so a breach is very hard to prove. Replace it with a schedule that can be checked against a log.
Example response
Proposed wording:
1. Lobby: vacuum and mop floors, wipe glass doors and letterbox fronts – daily (Monday to Friday).
2. Lifts: wipe internal walls, buttons and mirrors; vacuum floor – three times weekly (Monday, Wednesday, Friday).
3. Stairwells (east and west, levels 1–5): sweep and spot-mop – weekly; wipe handrails – weekly.
4. Basement car park: blow or sweep driveways and remove litter – fortnightly; remove oil spills within 2 business days of being reported.
5. Bin room: hose floor and wipe bin lids – weekly (after collection day).
6. Pool deck: sweep and remove litter, wipe outdoor furniture – three times weekly.
7. The caretaker will record the date of each task in the maintenance log, available to the committee on request.
Before it takes effect: legal review, deed of variation, and approval by the required resolution.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Covers area, task, standard and frequency for each area.
- Includes a way to verify performance (log).
- Recognises a formal variation process is required.
Not yet competent:
- Replaces the clause with another vague phrase ("regularly", "to a high standard").
Source gap: The training does not set out which resolution type is required to vary caretaking duties. Confirm against the applicable regulation module and legal advice before telling a committee what resolution to use.

title: "Resident unit manager" who doesn't live onsite
scenario: An owner at Sandpiper Place CTS 31207 complains: "Our resident unit manager lives in Carindale. He's in breach and should be removed." The agreement front page is titled "Resident Unit Manager Agreement". Clause 6 says: "The Caretaker must be available on site between 8.00 am and 5.00 pm Monday to Friday." No clause requires the caretaker to live in a lot. The manager attends site 8.00 am to 5.00 pm weekdays.
instructions:
1.	State whether living off site is a breach.
2.	Identify what you would check.
3.	Draft a reply to the owner.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Search the whole agreement for any residence clause (definitions, duties, letting authorisation, special conditions).
2.	Check any variation or deed adding a residence requirement.
3.	Check whether a letting authorisation or by-law imposes a residence condition.
4.	Check actual compliance with clause 6 (attendance hours).
Correct outcome: No breach. The title "Resident Unit Manager" does not create an obligation to reside. The enforceable obligation is clause 6 (on site 8–5 weekdays), which is being met.
Example response
Dear [Owner],
Thanks for raising this. I've reviewed the agreement. Although it is titled "Resident Unit Manager Agreement", it does not contain a term requiring the manager to live in the building. Clause 6 requires him to be on site from 8.00 am to 5.00 pm, Monday to Friday, and our information is that he is meeting those hours.
On that basis there is no breach. If you're aware of times when he hasn't been on site during those hours, please send me the dates and I'll look into it.
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Distinguishes the title from the operative terms.
- Checks for a residence clause across the whole agreement and any variations.
- Redirects the owner to the obligation that does exist.
Not yet competent:
- Agrees there is a breach because of the title.

title: Extra services by the previous caretaker
scenario: The management rights at Lakeview Gardens CTS 27731 have just been sold. The committee emails: "The old caretaker always washed down the driveway weekly and collected parcels for owners. The new caretaker must keep doing this." Neither task appears in Schedule 2. There is no deed of variation on file.
instructions:
1.	Advise whether the new caretaker is obliged to continue these services.
2.	Set out the committee's options.
3.	Draft the advice email.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Confirm the tasks are not in Schedule 2 or any variation.
2.	Check committee minutes and correspondence for any formal agreement with the previous caretaker (versus a goodwill arrangement).
3.	Confirm the assignment transferred the existing agreement on its existing terms.
Correct outcome: The new caretaker is not obliged to continue. Voluntary extra services do not become contractual duties. Options: ask the new caretaker to continue voluntarily, negotiate a formal variation (possibly with a fee adjustment) or engage a contractor.
Example response
Hi [Committee],
I've checked the agreement and file. Driveway wash-downs and parcel collection are not in the duty schedule, and there's no variation adding them. The previous caretaker did these voluntarily, so they don't carry over to the new caretaker.
Options:
1. Ask the new caretaker if they're willing to continue on a goodwill basis (can be stopped at any time).
2. Negotiate a formal variation adding the duties – this needs legal review and the appropriate resolution, and the caretaker may seek extra remuneration.
3. Get a quote from a contractor for the driveway wash-down.
Let me know how you'd like to proceed.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Concludes no obligation and explains why (not in agreement, no variation).
- Gives practical options including a formal variation.
Not yet competent:
- Says the new caretaker "should" continue because it's established practice.

title: Five-year top-up request
scenario: The caretaker at Ocean Crest CTS 33018 writes on 1 October requesting a five-year top-up of the term (current term expires 30 June 2034). The committee asks you: "What do we need to do and how long will it take?" The AGM is due in March 2027.
instructions:
1.	List the process steps in the correct order.
2.	Identify who is responsible for each step.
3.	Draft a short process summary for the committee.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Confirm the request is in writing and states the term sought.
2.	Obtain legal review of the agreement and the proposed deed of variation.
3.	Prepare the deed of variation.
4.	Decide whether to hold an EGM or include the motion at the AGM.
5.	Prepare the motion and explanatory material; include the secret-ballot arrangements and appoint a returning officer.
6.	Issue the notice of meeting.
7.	Conduct the meeting and ballot; returning officer counts and reports the result.
8.	Record the result in the minutes; if passed, execute the deed and file all documents (see Task 8).
Correct outcome: A top-up requires legal review, a deed of variation and a general-meeting decision by secret ballot with a returning officer. It cannot be decided by the committee alone.
Example response
Process summary for the committee:
1. Legal review of the agreement and proposed deed – body corporate solicitor.
2. Deed of variation prepared – solicitor, with the body corporate manager coordinating.
3. Committee decides whether to call an EGM now or include it at the March 2027 AGM.
4. Motion, explanatory note and secret-ballot papers prepared; returning officer appointed – body corporate manager.
5. Notice of meeting issued – body corporate manager.
6. Meeting held; returning officer counts and reports the ballot – returning officer.
7. Minutes record the result; if approved, deed signed and all records filed – body corporate manager.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Steps in a logical order with legal review before the motion.
- Identifies the secret ballot and returning officer.
- Identifies it as a general-meeting decision.
Not yet competent:
- Suggests the committee can approve it.
- Omits the secret ballot or the deed.
Source gap: The training does not state the resolution type needed to pass a top-up, the notice period for the meeting, or any statutory limit on the term. Confirm against the applicable legislation and legal advice before giving the committee a timeline.

title: Top-up motion that allows proxies
scenario: You are QA-checking the draft EGM papers for Ocean Crest CTS 33018. Motion 3 reads: "That the body corporate approves the five-year top-up of the caretaking agreement as per the attached deed." The voting paper for Motion 3 includes the standard box: "Proxy may vote on this motion." There is no reference to a secret ballot or returning officer.
instructions:
1.	Identify every problem with the motion and voting paper.
2.	State the correction required.
3.	Write the QA note to the preparer.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Voting method: training states a caretaker top-up requires a secret ballot without proxies.
2.	Ballot arrangements: returning officer appointed and named.
3.	Attachment: correct deed version attached.
4.	Motion wording: identifies the agreement, the new expiry date and authority to execute the deed.
Correct outcome: The papers cannot issue. The proxy option must be removed, secret-ballot papers and returning-officer arrangements added, and the motion wording tightened.
Example response
QA note – Ocean Crest EGM, Motion 3
Not approved for issue. Please correct:
1. Remove "Proxy may vote" for Motion 3 – proxies can't be used for a caretaker top-up.
2. Add secret-ballot voting paper and instructions, and name the returning officer.
3. Reword the motion to state the agreement date, the new expiry date (30 June 2039) and authority for two committee members to sign the deed.
4. Confirm the attached deed is the solicitor's final version (currently marked "Draft v2").
Return for re-check once updated.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Identifies the proxy problem and the missing secret ballot/returning officer.
- Gives specific corrections, not just "fix the motion".
Not yet competent:
- Only identifies the proxy issue as "possibly a problem".
Source gap: The training states the no-proxy/secret-ballot rule but does not cite the provision. Confirm the source provision before relying on it in written advice.

title: Filing after an approved top-up
scenario: The Ocean Crest top-up was approved at the EGM on 14 September. The deed was signed on 28 September. You have: the notice and motion, the returning officer's report, the ballot papers, the minutes, the signed deed, the solicitor's advice and invoice, and email correspondence with the caretaker.
instructions:
1.	Prepare a filing checklist.
2.	Identify any outstanding item that stops the file being closed.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Notice of meeting and motion (final issued version).
2.	Voting results and returning officer's report; ballot papers retained.
3.	Minutes recording the result.
4.	Signed deed of variation (all parties).
5.	Legal advice.
6.	Correspondence with the caretaker.
7.	Charges: solicitor's invoice and any disbursements, and whether any are recoverable from the caretaker.
8.	Agreement register updated with the new expiry date.
Correct outcome: All items listed must be on file and the agreement register updated before the matter is closed.
Example response
Filing checklist – Ocean Crest top-up
[ ] Notice of EGM and Motion 3 (as issued)
[ ] Returning officer's report and ballot papers
[ ] EGM minutes
[ ] Signed deed of variation (dated 28 September)
[ ] Solicitor's advice
[ ] Caretaker correspondence (request through to execution)
[ ] Solicitor's invoice and confirmation of who bears the cost
[ ] Agreement register updated: expiry now 30 June 2039
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Includes ballot/returning officer evidence and the signed deed.
- Includes updating the agreement expiry.
Not yet competent:
- Lists only "the minutes and deed".
Source gap: The training does not specify the storage location for agreement documents, how long ballot papers must be retained, or who bears the legal costs. Confirm against the internal filing procedure and the agreement.

title: Option clause exercisable "at any time"
scenario: Clause 4.2 of a caretaking agreement reads: "The Caretaker may exercise the option for a further term at any time." The current term expires 30 June 2028.
instructions:
1.	Explain the risk in this wording.
2.	Draft improved wording.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Identify the uncertainty: no start or end date for exercising the option, and no required form of notice.
2.	Identify consequences: the body corporate can't plan, there may be disputes about whether notice was given, and the option could be exercised long before expiry.
3.	Draft a defined written-notice window tied to the expiry date.
Correct outcome: The wording is uncertain and invites dispute. Replace it with a defined written-notice window.
Example response
Improved wording:
"4.2 The Caretaker may exercise the option for a further term only by giving written notice to the body corporate no earlier than six months and no later than three months before the expiry of the current term. Notice must be given in accordance with clause [notices clause]. If notice is not given within that period, the option lapses."
Note: the six-month/three-month window is an example only – the actual window must be settled with the body corporate's solicitor.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Identifies the uncertainty and at least one practical consequence.
- Provides wording with a start date, end date, form of notice and consequence of missing it.
Not yet competent:
- Says "make it clearer" without drafting.
Source gap: The training does not set a standard notice window. Any window must be settled on legal advice.

title: Assessing an inexperienced incoming caretaker
scenario: The proposed purchaser of the management rights at Bayside Lofts CTS 35560 has worked in hospitality management for 12 years but has never held management rights. The duties include pool maintenance, gardening, minor repairs and after-hours call-outs. The committee asks how it should assess the request for consent.
instructions:
1.	List the factors the committee should assess.
2.	Identify what evidence to request for each.
3.	Recommend how the committee documents its decision.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Capacity to perform the existing duties (not new ones).
2.	References from previous employers.
3.	Relevant qualifications or training (e.g. pool chemical handling, first aid).
4.	Financial capacity to operate the business.
5.	Probity checks (e.g. criminal history check).
6.	Interview with the committee.
7.	Support arrangements: training, mentoring by the outgoing caretaker, a handover period.
Correct outcome: Lack of prior management-rights experience is not on its own a reason to refuse. The committee should assess capacity to perform the existing duties using evidence, and record its reasons.
Example response
Recommendation to the committee:
Please assess the purchaser against the existing duties only. We recommend requesting: two employment references; evidence of any pool or first-aid training (or a plan to complete it before settlement); evidence of financial capacity; a criminal history check; and details of the handover/training proposed with the outgoing caretaker. A short interview is recommended. The committee's decision and reasons should be recorded in minutes.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Assesses against existing duties.
- Lists evidence for each factor and recommends recording reasons.
Not yet competent:
- Recommends refusal because of inexperience.
Source gap: The training does not state the time limit for the committee to decide on consent, or the grounds on which consent may lawfully be refused. Obtain legal advice before advising on refusal.

title: Due-diligence request for a purchaser
scenario: You receive notice that a buyer has signed a contract for the management rights at Bayside Lofts CTS 35560. The committee asks you to request the information it needs.
instructions:
1.	Draft the due-diligence request letter to the purchaser (or their solicitor).
2.	Set a response date.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Resume and references.
2.	Criminal history check.
3.	Licence evidence (where the letting business requires a licence).
4.	Evidence of financial capacity.
5.	Plant and equipment inventory.
6.	Master-key register and confirmation of key handover.
Correct outcome: A written request covering all items, with a response date, sent to the purchaser's solicitor.
Example response
Dear [Purchaser's solicitor],
Re: Proposed assignment – Bayside Lofts CTS 35560
To allow the committee to consider consent, please provide by [date – 10 business days]:
1. The purchaser's resume and two references.
2. A current criminal history check.
3. Evidence of any licence held or applied for.
4. Evidence of financial capacity to operate the business.
5. An inventory of plant and equipment to be transferred.
6. Confirmation of the master-key register and handover arrangements.
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Includes all six items and a response date.
Not yet competent:
- Missing the master-key register or financial capacity.
Source gap: The response period is an example only. The training does not set a deadline and the statutory timeframe for deciding consent is not covered.

title: New duties as a condition of assignment
scenario: The committee at Bayside Lofts writes: "We'll approve the sale only if the new caretaker agrees to clean windows monthly." Window cleaning is not a current duty.
instructions:
1.	Advise the committee.
2.	Suggest a lawful alternative.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Confirm window cleaning is not in the agreement.
2.	Identify what an assignment does: transfers the existing agreement on existing terms.
3.	Identify the risk of imposing conditions on consent.
Correct outcome: The committee should not make consent conditional on new duties. Any new duty should be negotiated separately as a variation.
Example response
Hi [Committee],
An assignment transfers the existing agreement as it stands. Making consent conditional on new duties such as monthly window cleaning isn't appropriate and could expose the body corporate to a dispute. Please assess the purchaser against the current duties. If you'd like window cleaning added, we can raise a separate variation with the new caretaker after settlement, which would need legal review and the proper resolution.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Clear "no" with the reason and an alternative.
Not yet competent:
- Suggests negotiating it into the consent.
Source gap: The training does not address the legal consequences of an unreasonable refusal or conditional consent. Obtain legal advice if the committee insists.

title: Committee wants an immediate remedial action notice
scenario: The chair at Parkside Terraces CTS 38870 emails: "Issue a remedial action notice today for the gardens. We've had enough." This follows Task 2; the caretaker's records have not yet been received.
instructions:
1.	Set out your recommended first steps, in order.
2.	Draft your reply to the chair.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Identify the specific contractual duty allegedly breached.
2.	Collect evidence (logs, photos, dates).
3.	Discuss with the caretaker and seek resolution.
4.	Consider training, negotiation or a written warning.
5.	Obtain specialist legal advice before any remedial action notice.
Correct outcome: Do not issue a notice today. Complete the evidence and resolution steps first and obtain legal advice before issuing.
Example response
Hi [Chair],
I understand the frustration. Before a remedial action notice can be issued safely, we need to (1) identify the exact duty breached, (2) gather the caretaker's records – requested, due Friday, (3) discuss the issues with him, and (4) get legal advice. A notice that is wrong in form or substance can be challenged and set back the body corporate's position. I'll report back after Friday with the evidence and a recommendation.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Lists steps in order with legal advice before the notice.
Not yet competent:
- Issues or drafts the notice immediately.
Source gap: The training does not cover the required content of a remedial action notice, the minimum period to remedy or the resolution needed to issue one. These must come from legal advice.

title: Budget to levy notices
scenario: Riverbend Apartments CTS 40112 has a financial year from 1 January. The AGM is scheduled for 24 November 2026. The draft budgets show an administrative fund of $233,000 and a sinking fund of $78,100. The scheme has 1,250 contribution entitlements.
instructions:
1.	List the steps from preparing the budget to issuing levy notices, in order.
2.	Calculate the annual rate per entitlement for each fund.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Prepare draft budgets and review against the prior year and sinking fund forecast.
2.	Committee considers the draft budgets.
3.	Budgets included in the AGM notice and approved at the AGM.
4.	Calculate the rate per entitlement for each fund.
5.	Verify the levy table: periods, rates and totals reconcile to the budget.
6.	Issue levy notices.
Correct outcome: Admin rate: $233,000 ÷ 1,250 = $186.40 per entitlement. Sinking rate: $78,100 ÷ 1,250 = $62.48 per entitlement. Total $248.88 per entitlement per year.
Example response
Rates for Riverbend (subject to AGM approval):
Administrative fund: $233,000 ÷ 1,250 = $186.40
Sinking fund: $78,100 ÷ 1,250 = $62.48
Total: $248.88 per entitlement per year
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Steps in order, with AGM approval before issue.
- Correct calculations.
Not yet competent:
- Issues notices before AGM approval.
- Calculation errors.

title: Calculating a lot's levy
scenario: Lot 7 at Riverbend Apartments has 20 contribution entitlements. The approved total rate is $248.88 per entitlement per year (admin $186.40, sinking $62.48). Levies are payable in four equal quarterly instalments.
instructions:
1.	Calculate the annual levy for lot 7, split by fund.
2.	Calculate the quarterly instalment.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Confirm the lot's entitlement figure from the CMS schedule.
2.	Multiply each fund rate by 20.
3.	Divide by four.
Correct outcome: Annual: admin 20 × $186.40 = $3,728.00; sinking 20 × $62.48 = $1,249.60; total $4,977.60. Quarterly: $1,244.40.
Example response
Lot 7 (20 entitlements):
Admin: $3,728.00 p.a. ($932.00 per quarter)
Sinking: $1,249.60 p.a. ($312.40 per quarter)
Total: $4,977.60 p.a. ($1,244.40 per quarter)
markingGuide:
Competent:
- All figures correct and split by fund.
Not yet competent:
- Arithmetic errors or no fund split.

title: Auditing a four-period levy table
scenario: The approved admin rate for Riverbend is $186.40 per entitlement. The levy table for the admin fund shows: Period 1 $46.60, Period 2 $46.60, Period 3 $46.60, Period 4 $46.50. Total entitlements: 1,250.
instructions:
1.	Audit the table against the approved rate.
2.	Quantify any error at scheme level.
3.	State the correction.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Add the four period rates: $46.60 + $46.60 + $46.60 + $46.50 = $186.30.
2.	Compare with the approved rate: $186.40. Difference $0.10 per entitlement.
3.	Scheme impact: $0.10 × 1,250 = $125.00 under-levied.
4.	Correct period 4 to $46.60 and re-check the total.
Correct outcome: The table is under by $0.10 per entitlement ($125.00 across the scheme). Correct period 4 to $46.60 before notices issue.
Example response
Audit note: Admin levy table totals $186.30 against approved $186.40. Period 4 is $46.50; should be $46.60. Under-levy $125.00 across 1,250 entitlements. Please correct and return for re-check.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Finds the period 4 error and quantifies it.
Not yet competent:
- Only says "table doesn't reconcile".

title: Explaining a levy increase to owners
scenario: Lot 7 paid $4,620.00 last year and will pay $4,977.60 this year. At scheme level, the admin budget rose from $213,750 to $233,000: CPI adjustments to contracts accounted for $7,500, and reinstated pool expenses (previously suspended during refurbishment) accounted for $11,750. The sinking fund rose from $75,000 to $78,100 in line with the forecast.
instructions:
1.	Calculate the dollar and percentage increase for lot 7.
2.	Draft a short owner explanation.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Lot increase: $4,977.60 − $4,620.00 = $357.60.
2.	Percentage: $357.60 ÷ $4,620.00 = 7.74%.
3.	Check that the reasons reconcile: $7,500 + $11,750 = $19,250 = admin increase; sinking increase $3,100; total $22,350.
Correct outcome: Increase of $357.60 (7.74%), explained by CPI adjustments, reinstated pool costs and the forecast sinking fund increase.
Example response
Why have levies gone up?
Your levies have increased by 7.74% this year (for a 20-entitlement lot, from $4,620.00 to $4,977.60, or $357.60). The reasons:
- CPI increases to existing contracts: $7,500 across the building.
- Pool running costs back in the budget after the refurbishment: $11,750.
- A $3,100 increase to the sinking fund, in line with the 10-year forecast.
markingGuide:
Competent:

title: Special levy dates
scenario: The committee at Coral Point CTS 29455 proposes a $90,000 special levy for balcony repairs, payable in two instalments on 15 December and 15 March. Ordinary levies are due 1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October.

Hi [Committee],
I recommend the special levy instalments align with the ordinary levy dates – 1 January and 1 April instead of 15 December and 15 March. title: Special levy QC checklist
scenario: You are about to QC the Coral Point special levy before issue: resolution passed at EGM on 2 October for $90,000 for balcony repairs, payable in two equal instalments 1 January and 1 April, levied on contribution entitlements (total 900).
instructions:

Checks in order

2.	Fund: admin or sinking as stated in the resolution.

4.	Instalments: number and amount.
5.	Issue dates and due dates.
6.	Reconciliation: total levied equals $90,000.

QC checklist – Coral Point special levy
[ ] Resolution date 2 October; amount $90,000; purpose balcony repairs
[ ] Fund as per resolution
[ ] Contribution schedule used (900 entitlements)
[ ] 2 instalments × $50.00 per entitlement

Competent:

title: Expected levy receipts with discount

title: Negative balance on an aged-balance report

Levy notice for the 15 January 2027 period to issue on 4 December 2026, showing the amount (with discount if paid by due date), due date and payment options.

title: Lot approaching escalation
scenario: Lot 18 at Riverbend owes $3,840.55, now 95 days overdue. The committee meets on 20 October.

title: Scheme emails in a personal mailbox
scenario: The treasurer of Lakeview Gardens CTS 27731 has been emailing two roofing contractors from her personal Gmail account to arrange quotes for roof repairs (quotes of $18,400 and $21,950). An owner has asked to see "all correspondence about the roof quotes". The treasurer says: "Those are my personal emails, not body corporate records."
instructions:
1.	Assess whether the emails are body corporate records, giving your reason.
2.	State what the treasurer should do now and in future.
3.	Draft your email to the treasurer.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Content: do the emails deal with body corporate business (quotes for common property repairs)?
2.	Purpose: were they sent in her role as a committee member, on behalf of the body corporate?
3.	Storage: note that where the emails are stored does not decide their status.
4.	Next step: obtain copies so they can be filed and assessed against the owner's request.
Correct outcome: The emails are likely body corporate records because their content and purpose relate to body corporate business; the fact they are in a personal mailbox does not change that. The treasurer should forward copies to the body corporate manager for filing, and copy the manager into body corporate correspondence from now on.
Example response
Hi [Treasurer],
Thanks for your work on the roof quotes. Emails about body corporate business – such as arranging the $18,400 and $21,950 roof quotes – are likely to be body corporate records, even though they're in your personal mailbox. What counts is what the emails are about and why they were sent, not where they're stored.
Could you please forward the full email chains with both contractors (including attachments) to me by Friday? We'll file them and assess them against the owner's request.
Going forward, it's best to copy me into any body corporate correspondence so the record is complete.
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Applies the content-and-purpose test and states that location is not decisive.
- Asks for the full chains, including attachments, to be filed.
- Gives a forward-looking fix (copy the manager in).
Not yet competent:
- Accepts that a personal mailbox makes them personal records.
- Says they "may be" records without a reason or next step.

title: Committee decisions by WhatsApp
scenario: The five-member committee at Sandpiper Place CTS 31207 uses a WhatsApp group that the body corporate manager is not part of. On 22 September the chair posted: "Shall we approve the $4,800 gate repair quote from SecureGate?" Four members replied "Agree". The chair has now emailed you: "Committee approved the gate quote – please issue the work order."
instructions:
1.	Explain the records implications of the WhatsApp messages.
2.	Identify whether a valid committee decision has been made.
3.	Draft your reply to the chair.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Records: the messages concern body corporate business, so they may form part of the body corporate record.
2.	Retention: the messages need to be exported and filed with the body corporate manager.
3.	Decision: check whether the decision was made at a committee meeting or by a properly issued VOC. A chat thread is neither.
4.	Action: do not issue the work order until a valid decision exists.
Correct outcome: The messages may be body corporate records and should be exported and filed. Agreement in a chat group is not a valid committee decision. The work order should not issue until the decision is made by VOC or at a meeting.
Example response
Hi [Chair],
Thanks for letting me know. Two things:
1. Messages in the WhatsApp group that deal with body corporate business may be body corporate records. Please export the chat (or at least the gate discussion) and send it to me for filing.
2. Agreement in the chat group isn't a valid committee decision, so I can't issue the work order yet. I'll prepare a VOC for the $4,800 SecureGate quote today. Once the VOC has run its course and is minuted, I'll issue the work order.
If the gate is a security risk in the meantime, let me know and we'll look at whether urgent temporary measures are needed.
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Addresses both the records issue and the invalid decision.
- Refuses to issue the work order and gives the correct path (VOC or meeting).
Not yet competent:
- Issues the work order based on the chat.
- Addresses only one of the two issues.
Source gap: The training does not explain how messaging-app records should be exported, stored or retained, or whether any urgent-works exception applies. Confirm the internal procedure.

title: Owner requests retained CCTV
scenario: On 15 September a parked car was scratched in the basement at Coral Point CTS 29455. The building manager saved the CCTV footage from 2.00 pm to 4.00 pm that day to a USB drive; the system otherwise overwrites footage after 30 days. On 1 October the owner of lot 22 (who is not the car owner) emails: "Please send me a copy of the CCTV from the incident."
instructions:
1.	List, in order, the issues you must assess before responding.
2.	State the immediate action to take today.
3.	Draft an acknowledgement to the owner.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Preserve first: confirm the USB copy exists, is stored securely and is not at risk of being deleted.
2.	Is the request in writing and does it meet the records-request requirements (see Task 31)?
3.	Does the retained footage form part of the body corporate record?
4.	Does lot 22's owner have a right of access to it?
5.	Privacy and disclosure: other residents and the car owner are identifiable in the footage.
6.	Decide on access only after these checks, with advice if needed.
Correct outcome: Preserve the footage today and acknowledge the request. Do not release or refuse until access rights and privacy concerns have been assessed.
Example response
Dear [Owner],
Thank you for your request of 1 October for CCTV footage relating to the incident in the basement on 15 September. The footage has been preserved. We are assessing your request, including whether the footage forms part of the body corporate records and any privacy considerations for other people shown in it. We will respond once that assessment is complete.
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Preserves the footage as the first step.
- Identifies record status, access rights and privacy as separate issues.
- Neither releases nor refuses on the spot.
Not yet competent:
- Sends the footage straight away or refuses without assessment.
- Overlooks the 30-day overwrite risk.
Source gap: The training identifies the issues but does not state the legal position on owner access to CCTV, the privacy obligations that apply, or the timeframe to respond. Obtain advice before releasing footage.

title: Committee proposes deleting CCTV after a request
scenario: Following Task 28, the Coral Point chair emails: "Just delete the footage. It's not worth the hassle and the system would have overwritten it by now anyway."
instructions:
1.	Advise the chair against deletion.
2.	Explain the risk in plain words.
3.	State what happens next.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	A request for the footage has been received.
2.	Deleting material after a request has been made creates significant risk for the body corporate.
3.	The fact the system would normally have overwritten it does not matter – a copy was deliberately kept.
4.	The footage must be preserved pending proper assessment.
Correct outcome: The footage must not be deleted. It should be preserved while the request is assessed.
Example response
Hi [Chair],
I understand it's a nuisance, but we can't delete the footage now. A request has been received, and deleting material after that point creates significant risk for the body corporate. It doesn't help that the system would normally have overwritten it – a copy was deliberately kept, and it now needs to be dealt with properly.
We'll keep the footage secure while the request is assessed, and I'll come back to the committee with a recommendation on whether, and how, it can be released.
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Clear refusal with the reason.
- Deals with the "it would have been overwritten anyway" argument.
Not yet competent:
- Agrees to delete or leaves the decision to the committee without advice.

title: Auditing a staff member's filing for a disputed matter
scenario: The owner of lot 4 at Parkside Terraces is disputing a $1,200 charge for water damage repairs. The file has: (1) the owner's complaint email of 3 September, (2) the manager's reply of 5 September, and (3) the plumber's invoice. You know that: the plumber's original email attached a report and photos identifying the source of the leak; the committee approved recovering the cost from lot 4 by VOC on 20 August; and the owner sent a second email on 12 September with a quote from his own plumber.
instructions:
1.	Audit the file against what should be there.
2.	List each missing item and where to find it.
3.	Write the audit note to the staff member.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Incoming correspondence: both owner emails (3 and 12 September).
2.	Incoming attachments: the owner's plumber quote; the contractor's report and photos.
3.	Outgoing correspondence: the manager's reply of 5 September and any later reply.
4.	Decisions: the 20 August VOC notice, result and minutes.
5.	Supporting documents: invoice, report, photos.
Correct outcome: The file is incomplete. Missing: the owner's 12 September email and quote, the plumber's report and photos, and the VOC records. These must be filed before any further response to the owner.
Example response
Audit note – Lot 4 water damage dispute
The file is incomplete. Please file the following by close of business tomorrow:
1. Owner's email of 12 September and attached plumber's quote – check the scheme inbox.
2. Plumber's report and photos – attachments to his original email with the invoice.
3. VOC of 20 August approving recovery from lot 4 – notice, result and minutes.
Please don't send any further response to the owner until these are on file, as the report and VOC are the basis for the charge.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Identifies all three missing items.
- Checks attachments, not just emails.
- Holds further response until the file is complete.
Not yet competent:
- Says the file is complete because there are emails both ways and an invoice.
- Misses the decision record.

title: Assessing a records request for validity
scenario: Your office receives this email: "I'm buying unit 9 at Ocean Crest. Please send me the last three years of committee minutes. – J. Nguyen." No fee is attached and there is no authority from the owner of lot 9.
instructions:
1.	Assess the request against each validity requirement.
2.	State whether it can be processed now.
3.	Draft the response.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	In writing: yes (email).
2.	Sufficiently specific: yes – committee minutes, last three years.
3.	Eligible person: a prospective buyer is not the owner; check whether the owner's written authority or another basis applies.
4.	Prescribed fee: not paid.
Correct outcome: The request cannot be processed yet. Request evidence of eligibility (such as the owner's written authority) and the prescribed fee.
Example response
Dear J. Nguyen,
Thank you for your request for the last three years of committee minutes for Ocean Crest. Before we can process it, please provide:
1. Written authority from the owner of lot 9 for you to inspect the body corporate records; and
2. Payment of the prescribed fee of $[amount].
Once we receive both, we'll process your request.
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Tests all four requirements individually.
- Identifies both the eligibility and fee gaps.
Not yet competent:
- Sends the minutes.
- Refuses outright without explaining what's needed.
Source gap: The training refers to "eligible person" and "prescribed fee" but does not define who is eligible (for example, whether a buyer's agent or solicitor is) or state the fee amount. Confirm both against the current regulation and internal fee schedule.

title: "All records concerning the building"
scenario: The owner of lot 31 at Riverbend Apartments emails: "Under my rights as an owner, provide all records concerning the building." The scheme has been managed by your firm for 14 years.
instructions:
1.	Assess the request.
2.	Draft a response that helps the owner make a valid request.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	In writing: yes.
2.	Eligible: owner – yes.
3.	Specific: no – "all records concerning the building" doesn't identify documents or categories.
4.	Fee: not yet able to calculate, as the scope isn't known.
Correct outcome: The request is not sufficiently specific. Ask the owner to identify the documents or categories and date range sought.
Example response
Dear [Owner],

- committee and general meeting minutes for 2024–2026;
- the current insurance policy and valuation;
- contracts for cleaning and gardening.
Once we have that, we'll confirm the fee and process the request.
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Identifies lack of specificity as the problem.
- Gives examples and asks for a date range.
Not yet competent:
- Starts collecting everything, or refuses without helping the owner narrow it.

title: Valid requester hasn't paid the fee
scenario: The owner of lot 3 at Riverbend submits a written request on 28 September for (a) the 2025 AGM minutes and (b) the current building insurance schedule. No payment has been made.
instructions:

Checks in order

2.	Fee: not paid.

Dear [Owner],
Thank you for your request of 28 September for the 2025 AGM minutes and the current building insurance schedule. The prescribed fee for this request is $[amount]. We'll start processing as soon as payment is received.
Payment details: [BSB/account/reference or payment link].
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:

- States the fee and that processing starts on payment.
Not yet competent:

title: Owner asks the manager to create a five-year expenditure summary
scenario: The owner of lot 14 at Lakeview Gardens emails: "Please prepare a summary of all expenditure from 2021 to 2025 broken down by category so I can see where the money went." Audited financial statements exist for each year.

Checks in order
1.	Does a five-year summary already exist? No.

3.	Obligation: provide existing records on a valid request; no obligation to create a new report.
Correct outcome: The body corporate manager is not required to create a report that doesn't exist. The owner can request copies of the existing financial statements for 2021–2025.

Dear [Owner],

Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Distinguishes existing records from creating new ones.
- Offers the existing documents that meet the need.
Not yet competent:
- Agrees to prepare the summary, or refuses without offering the existing records.

title: Document with legal advice and allegations about an owner
scenario: The owner of lot 6 requests "all committee emails about my by-law breach". The emails include: (a) the solicitor's advice on the breach notice, forwarded to the committee; (b) a committee member's email saying the owner is "a known troublemaker who lies to everyone"; and (c) routine scheduling emails.

File note – Lot 6 records request
Request covers three categories:

- Separates the categories and gives the correct concern for each.

title: Internal worksheet later emailed to the committee

title: Records handover to a new manager
scenario: Sandpiper Place CTS 31207 has resolved to transfer management to another company from 1 November. Records include: current electronic folders, archived scanned files (pre-2018, not text-searchable), solicitor's advice, CCTV preserved for a pending request, and the master-key register.

title: Explaining CMS vs BMS to a new manager
scenario: A new manager has been given Harbour Quarter, a mixed-use site with three entities: a residential body corporate (CTS 41250), a commercial body corporate (CTS 41251) and a hotel lot owned by a separate company. The site has a community management statement (CMS) for each scheme and one building management statement (BMS) across all three. The manager asks: "Which document do I use for what?"
instructions:
1.	Explain the difference between the CMS and the BMS in plain words.
2.	Give one example from Harbour Quarter of an issue governed by each.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	CMS: governs the body corporate's own matters – lots, entitlements, by-laws, exclusive use.
2.	BMS: governs shared areas, shared services, maintenance responsibilities and cost allocation between the separate entities.
3.	Apply to the site with a concrete example of each.
Correct outcome: Use the CMS for matters inside the residential (or commercial) scheme; use the BMS for anything shared between the three entities.
Example response
Hi [Manager],
Quick guide for Harbour Quarter:
- CMS – the rule book for each body corporate on its own: lot entitlements, by-laws, exclusive use. Example: a residential owner's pet application is dealt with under the residential CMS by-laws.
- BMS – the agreement between the three entities for what they share: shared areas, shared services, who maintains what, and how costs are split. Example: the shared basement car park entry and its boom gate maintenance cost are dealt with under the BMS, using the percentages in its cost schedule.
If an issue involves more than one entity, start with the BMS.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Accurate distinction between the two documents.
- Correct example of each, applied to the site.
Not yet competent:
- Treats them as interchangeable or gives definitions with no example.

title: Assuming a new BMS works like another scheme
scenario: A manager who has looked after Harbour Quarter for two years takes on Southbank Junction, which also has a BMS. He has started allocating shared cleaning costs at 60/40, as he does at Harbour Quarter, without reading the Southbank BMS. The first quarter's recoveries ($14,200) were raised on that basis.
instructions:
1.	Identify the risk.
2.	State what should be done now.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Every BMS is unique: parties, shared areas, services and percentages differ.
2.	Southbank's BMS must be reviewed before any allocation or advice.
3.	Check the recoveries already raised against the correct percentages.
4.	Correct any errors and inform the affected entities.
Correct outcome: The manager may have allocated $14,200 on the wrong basis. Review the Southbank BMS now, recalculate the quarter and correct any difference before the next recovery.
Example response
Hi [Manager],
Each BMS is different, so Southbank's percentages can't be assumed from Harbour Quarter. Please review the Southbank BMS cost schedule today, recalculate the $14,200 cleaning recovery for the quarter using its percentages, and let me know the difference for each entity. We'll then correct the recovery and write to the entities explaining the adjustment.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Identifies the risk of wrong allocation and disputes.
- Requires the BMS review and a recalculation of what's already been raised.
Not yet competent:
- Says "check the BMS" without dealing with the recoveries already issued.

title: First-review checklist for a BMS
scenario: You have been handed the 86-page BMS for Southbank Junction and asked to summarise it for the team before the first BMG meeting.
instructions:
1.	Prepare a first-review checklist.
2.	For each item, state what you are recording.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Parties to the BMS and their representatives.
2.	Shared areas (with plan references).
3.	Shared services (e.g. fire systems, lifts, car park, waste).
4.	Maintenance responsibilities for each shared area and service.
5.	Cost-allocation percentages for each cost category.
6.	Voting rights of each party.
7.	Meeting requirements (frequency, notice, quorum).
8.	Dispute-resolution process.
Correct outcome: A one-page summary capturing each item with the clause reference, so the team can find the source quickly.
Example response
BMS first-review checklist – Southbank Junction
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Covers all eight items and records clause references.
Not yet competent:
- Misses cost percentages, voting or disputes.

title: Recovering a shared-area invoice paid by the body corporate
scenario: The residential body corporate at Harbour Quarter paid a $6,800 invoice for repairs to the shared driveway roller door. Under the BMS cost schedule, the driveway is a shared area split: residential 45%, commercial 35%, hotel 20%.
instructions:
1.	Confirm whether the cost is recoverable.
2.	Calculate each entity's share.
3.	State how the recovery is processed.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Confirm the driveway roller door is a shared area under the BMS.
2.	Confirm the repair falls within a cost category covered by the schedule.
3.	Apply the percentages: residential 45% = $3,060.00; commercial 35% = $2,380.00; hotel 20% = $1,360.00. Total $6,800.00.
4.	Raise recoveries for the commercial and hotel shares and record the residential share as its own cost.
Correct outcome: Recover $2,380.00 from the commercial body corporate and $1,360.00 from the hotel; the residential body corporate bears $3,060.00.
Example response
Recovery – Harbour Quarter driveway roller door (invoice $6,800.00)
Residential (45%): $3,060.00 – retained
Commercial (35%): $2,380.00 – recover
Hotel (20%): $1,360.00 – recover
Attach the invoice and BMS clause reference to each recovery.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Confirms the BMS covers the cost before recovering.
- Correct calculations that total $6,800.
Not yet competent:
- Splits the cost evenly or without confirming it is shared.

title: BMG administration fees without a current agreement
scenario: Your firm has charged the Harbour Quarter BMG an administration fee of $1,150 per month since January. The BMG administration agreement expired on 31 December last year and has not been renewed.
instructions:
1.	Identify the risk.
2.	State the action required.
3.	Draft a note to the BMG chair.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Confirm the expiry date and whether the agreement has a holding-over clause.
2.	Calculate fees charged since expiry: January to September = 9 months × $1,150 = $10,350.
3.	Risk: fees may be disputed or reversed.
4.	Action: establish or renew a valid agreement and confirm authority for fees already charged.
Correct outcome: $10,350 in fees has been charged without a current agreement and could be disputed or reversed. Renew the agreement and seek confirmation of the fees charged since January.
Example response
Hi [BMG chair],
Our administration agreement with the BMG expired on 31 December. We've continued providing services and charging $1,150 per month since January ($10,350 to the end of September). To put this on a proper footing, we'll send a renewal agreement this week, and ask the BMG to confirm the fees charged since January as part of approving it.
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Quantifies the exposure and identifies the risk.
- Proposes renewal and confirmation of past fees.
Not yet competent:
- Continues charging without raising it.
Source gap: The training does not state whether the expired agreement's terms continue to apply, or the internal escalation process for fees charged without authority. Check the agreement and internal procedure.

title: Year-end BMG wash-up
scenario: Harbour Quarter's BMG estimated shared expenses for the year at $120,000 and recovered quarterly on that basis: residential 45% ($54,000), commercial 35% ($42,000), hotel 20% ($24,000). Actual shared expenses were $131,600.
instructions:
1.	Calculate each entity's actual share.
2.	Calculate the wash-up adjustment for each.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Actual shares: residential 45% × $131,600 = $59,220; commercial 35% = $46,060; hotel 20% = $26,320.
2.	Adjustments: residential $59,220 − $54,000 = $5,220; commercial $46,060 − $42,000 = $4,060; hotel $26,320 − $24,000 = $2,320.
3.	Total additional $11,600 = $131,600 − $120,000.
Correct outcome: Each entity owes an additional amount: residential $5,220, commercial $4,060, hotel $2,320 (total $11,600).
Example response
BMG wash-up – Harbour Quarter
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Correct calculations that reconcile to the overspend.
Not yet competent:
- Splits the overspend evenly, or calculation errors.
Source gap: The training does not say how the adjustment is invoiced or credited, or whether it carries into the next year's budget. Confirm the internal procedure.

title: Supporting schedule for BMG recoveries in AGM papers
scenario: The residential body corporate at Harbour Quarter has its AGM in November. Owners have asked why the BMG recoveries line in the budget increased. You need to prepare the supporting schedule using the Task 44 figures.
instructions:
1.	Prepare the schedule for the AGM papers.
2.	Add a one-line note explaining the adjustment.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Expenses by category.
2.	Allocation rule (percentage and BMS clause).
3.	Participating entities.
4.	Amounts already recovered.
5.	Final adjustments.
Correct outcome: A schedule showing the shared expenses, allocation basis, amounts already paid and the $5,220 adjustment owed by the residential body corporate.
Example response
BMG shared expenses – year ended [date]
Total actual shared expenses: $131,600 (estimate $120,000)
Residential share (45% under BMS cl. [x]): $59,220
Already paid in quarterly contributions: $54,000
Adjustment payable: $5,220
Note: Shared expenses were $11,600 above estimate, mainly due to [main reason from the expense breakdown].
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Includes all five elements and the reason for the variance.
Not yet competent:
- Shows a total with no allocation basis.

title: Unanimous approval required and one party refuses
scenario: Under the Southbank Junction BMS, replacing the shared fire panel ($62,000) requires unanimous approval of the BMG. The residential and commercial representatives have voted yes; the hotel representative has refused, saying the quote is too high.
instructions:
1.	Recommend the next steps in order.
2.	Draft a note to the BMG.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Confirm the BMS requires unanimous approval for this item.
2.	Review the BMS dispute-resolution clause and its steps.
3.	Explore the reason for refusal: obtain additional quotes if price is the issue.
4.	Negotiation first, then the steps in the dispute clause (e.g. legal advice, independent expert determination).
5.	Consider compliance risk if the fire panel is required to be replaced.
Correct outcome: Follow the BMS dispute process: address the hotel's objection (more quotes), negotiate, and if unresolved, use the dispute mechanism specified in the BMS.
Example response
Hi all,
The fire panel replacement needs unanimous approval under the BMS, and the hotel has not approved because of price. Proposed next steps:
1. Obtain two further quotes within 3 weeks.
2. Reconvene the BMG to consider all quotes.
3. If agreement still isn't reached, follow the dispute process in clause [x] of the BMS.
Given the fire safety implications, we'll also confirm with the fire contractor whether any interim measures are needed.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Uses the BMS dispute clause, addresses the reason for refusal, and considers safety.
Not yet competent:
- Proceeds without unanimous approval, or stops at "the motion failed".
Source gap: The training does not state the specific dispute-resolution steps for any BMS – these must come from the BMS itself.

title: Invoice incorrectly treated as body corporate-only
scenario: A $2,450 invoice for servicing the shared fire pump at Harbour Quarter was coded to the residential body corporate's fire safety account and paid in full. The fire pump is a shared service under the BMS (residential 45%, commercial 35%, hotel 20%).
instructions:
1.	Explain the correction process.
2.	Calculate the recovery.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Confirm the fire pump is a shared service under the BMS.
2.	Correct the coding to the BMG recovery account.
3.	Calculate the recovery: commercial 35% = $857.50; hotel 20% = $490.00; residential retains 45% = $1,102.50.
4.	Raise recoveries and file the supporting documents.
Correct outcome: Recode the invoice and recover $857.50 from the commercial body corporate and $490.00 from the hotel.
Example response
Correction – fire pump service invoice $2,450.00
1. Recode from residential fire safety to BMG shared services.
2. Recover commercial $857.50 and hotel $490.00.
3. Residential share $1,102.50.
4. File invoice and BMS clause with the recoveries.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Confirms shared status, recodes and calculates correctly.
Not yet competent:
- Leaves the coding and only raises a recovery, or vice versa.

title: BMG dispute over voting rights and repair costs
scenario: The commercial representative at Southbank Junction says she has two votes on the BMG because the commercial scheme has more floor area, and that the hotel should pay 50% of a $28,000 car park repair "because hotel guests use it most". The BMS gives each party one vote and splits car park costs residential 50%, commercial 30%, hotel 20%.
instructions:
1.	Analyse each claim against the BMS.
2.	Prepare your advice.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Voting provisions: one vote per party.
2.	Cost schedule: car park split 50/30/20.
3.	Decision requirements for the repair (majority or unanimous?).
4.	Dispute-resolution process if a party wants to change the allocation.
Correct outcome: Both claims are inconsistent with the BMS. Each party has one vote, and the car park repair is split residential $14,000, commercial $8,400, hotel $5,600. Any change to the allocation needs an amendment to the BMS.
Example response
Hi [Commercial representative],
I've reviewed the BMS:
- Voting: each party has one vote (clause [x]). Floor area does not change this.
- Car park costs: split 50/30/20 (clause [y]). For the $28,000 repair: residential $14,000, commercial $8,400, hotel $5,600.
Usage by hotel guests doesn't change the allocation. If you'd like to propose a different split, that would need an amendment to the BMS, and we can discuss the process.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Tests each claim against the BMS and gives the correct allocation.
Not yet competent:
- Gives an opinion on fairness without the BMS terms.
Source gap: The training does not explain the process to amend a BMS. Seek legal advice if a party wants to pursue it.

title: "Approved" in the invoice system – was it paid?
scenario: A contractor calls about invoice #4471 ($3,280 for gutter cleaning at Riverbend). The invoice approval system shows the status "Approved". The contractor says the money hasn't arrived.
instructions:
1.	Determine whether the invoice was paid.
2.	State what you'd tell the contractor.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	"Approved" means the invoice has been approved, not that it has been paid.
2.	Check the transaction history or the invoice details for an EFT entry.
3.	Confirm the paid status and a zero outstanding balance.
Correct outcome: "Approved" alone does not show payment. Payment is confirmed only by an EFT entry, paid status and zero outstanding balance.
Example response
Hi [Contractor],
Invoice #4471 has been approved. I've checked payment: [either] it was paid by EFT on [date], reference [EFT ref], and should be in your account; [or] it hasn't been paid yet – it's approved and will be included in the next payment run.
Kind regards,
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Distinguishes approved from paid and checks the payment record.
Not yet competent:
- Tells the contractor it's paid because it says "approved".

title: Payable invoice coded incorrectly – approval instruction
scenario: Invoice #5102 for $1,640 from Clearflow Plumbing at Lakeview Gardens is for repairing a burst pipe in the common property stairwell. It has been coded to 152 Garden Maintenance. It should be 158 Plumbing Repairs.
instructions: 1.	Draft the approval instruction.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Confirm the work was done and the amount is correct (payable).
2.	Approve the invoice.
3.	Add a clear instruction identifying the correct account name and number and why.
Correct outcome: Approve the invoice and add the recoding instruction.
Example response
Approval note: "Approved for payment. Please recode from 152 Garden Maintenance to 158 Plumbing Repairs – this is a burst pipe repair in the common property stairwell, not garden work."
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Approves and gives the specific account name and number and reason.
Not yet competent:
- Leaves it unapproved, or approves with no recoding note.

title: Why leaving the invoice unapproved isn't the answer
scenario: A colleague left invoice #5102 (Task 51) unapproved because the code was wrong. It's now 21 days old and Clearflow has called about payment.
instructions:
1.	Explain to the colleague why leaving it unapproved was not appropriate.
2.	State what to do now.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Leaving it unapproved puts it on hold.
2.	It also stops the normal recoding process from being completed.
3.	Result: the contractor isn't paid and the coding isn't fixed.
Correct outcome: Approve the invoice now with a recoding instruction (as in Task 51).
Example response
Hi [Colleague],
Leaving #5102 unapproved puts it on hold and stops the recoding from happening, so Clearflow hasn't been paid and the code is still wrong. When an invoice is payable but coded incorrectly, please approve it and add a clear recoding note. Could you do that today, and let Clearflow know it'll be in the next payment run?
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Gives both reasons and the correct action.
Not yet competent:
- Only says "it delays payment".

title: Improving the note "wrong code"
scenario: An approver added the note "wrong code" to an invoice for $480 for replacing pool deck lights at Coral Point, coded to 210 Pool Chemicals.
instructions: 1.	Rewrite the note.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Name the correct account and number.
2.	Give a brief reason.
Correct outcome: A note that states the correct account and reason.
Example response
"Approved. Please recode from 210 Pool Chemicals to 175 Electrical Repairs – replacement of pool deck lights, not chemicals."
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Includes the account name, number and reason.
Not yet competent:
- Still vague (e.g. "please fix code").
Source gap: The account numbers above are examples only. Use the scheme's chart of accounts.

title: Approver questions the amount but gives no instruction
scenario: An approver at Ocean Crest added the note "Seems high?" to a $9,800 invoice for lift repairs and approved nothing. The accounts payable team has queried what to do.
instructions:
1.	Identify who must follow up.
2.	Draft the instruction to the accounts payable team.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	The accounts payable team can't act on a question without an instruction.
2.	The responsible local team must investigate (compare to quote, contact contractor).
3.	Then specifically instruct the accounts payable team (approve, hold, partial payment).
Correct outcome: The local team is responsible for investigating and giving the accounts payable team a specific instruction.
Example response
Hi [accounts payable team],
We're checking the $9,800 lift repair invoice against the quote of $8,200. Please hold until we confirm by Wednesday. We'll then instruct you to either approve it in full or pay $8,200 pending a credit note.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Assigns responsibility to the local team and gives a specific instruction.
Not yet competent:
- Leaves it to the accounts payable team to decide.

title: Locating an older invoice in the transaction history
scenario: The owner of lot 9 at Riverbend asks for a copy of the invoice for painting the lobby in 2024. All you know is that the painter was BrightCoat Painters and the work was "sometime mid-2024". The invoice approval screen only shows the current year.
instructions:
1.	Describe the steps to locate the invoice.
2.	State what to do once it's found.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Open the transaction history (not the invoice approval screen, which only shows the current year).
2.	Select the correct financial year (2024).
3.	Search by creditor (BrightCoat Painters) or by the painting account code.
4.	Open the transaction details to view and download the invoice.
5.	Check whether the owner's request needs to be treated as a records request (Task 31) before sending.
Correct outcome: The invoice is found in the transaction history by selecting 2024 and searching by creditor or account code.
Example response
Steps:
1. Open the transaction history for Riverbend Apartments.
2. Change the year to 2024.
3. Search creditor "BrightCoat" (or filter by the painting account code).
4. Open the matching transaction(s) from mid-2024 and view the invoice.
5. Save a copy and process the owner's request through the records request process.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Selects the right year and search criteria, and opens transaction details.
- Recognises the records-request step.
Not yet competent:
- Searches only the current year on the invoice approval screen.
Source gap: The training does not say whether an owner's request for an invoice must go through the formal records request process. Confirm the internal procedure.

title: Verifying payment to a creditor
scenario: The committee asks you to confirm that Bayside Lofts paid GreenScape Gardens invoice #GG-2290 for $1,375.
instructions:
1.	List the verification steps.
2.	Draft the confirmation to the committee.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Locate the invoice.
2.	Confirm the EFT reference.
3.	Confirm paid status.
4.	Confirm zero outstanding amount.
Correct outcome: Payment is confirmed only when all three are present.
Example response
Hi [Committee],
GreenScape invoice #GG-2290 ($1,375.00) was paid by EFT on [date], reference [EFT ref]. The invoice shows as paid with nothing outstanding.
markingGuide:
Competent:
- Uses all three confirmations.
Not yet competent:
- Relies on one element only.

title: Creditor says unpaid but the ledger shows zero owing
scenario: SparkRight Electrical emails: "Invoice #8812 for $2,140 is 45 days overdue." The ledger shows the invoice paid by EFT on 28 August, reference EFT-77341, with zero owing.
instructions: 1.	Prepare your response.
modelAnswer:
Checks in order
1.	Confirm the EFT details (date, reference, amount, creditor bank account).
2.	Confirm the remittance was sent.
3.	Provide verified payment information to the creditor.
Correct outcome: Provide the EFT date, reference and amount, and the remittance.
Example response
Hi SparkRight,
Invoice #8812 for $2,140.00 was paid by EFT on 28 August, reference EFT-77341, to the account ending [last 4 digits]. A copy of the remittance is attached. Please check with your bank and let us know if it can't be located.

Competent:
- Confirms details before responding, including the bank account used.
Not yet competent:
- Re-pays or tells the creditor to check without giving details.

title: Journal selected instead of an invoice for recoding
scenario: A staff member trying to recode a $600 cleaning invoice at Riverbend has opened a journal entry (JNL-3302) instead of the invoice.
instructions: 1.	Explain the correct action.

title: Ten transactions require recoding
